title: Does Autonomy Change the Nature of War, or Only Its Character?
faculty_prompt:
Seminar 12,

This week's readings paired Clausewitz on friction, chance, and the culminating point with contemporary literature on autonomous systems, algorithmic decision support, and long-range precision fires.

Your issue for discussion:

A recurring claim in the current literature is that artificial intelligence and autonomous weapons are changing the nature of war rather than merely its character. Assess that claim.

Do not stop at asserting the distinction. If you argue the nature is immutable, tell the seminar what would falsify your position. posts.author: LtCol (Ret) J. Halloran
posts.subject: IFD 2: Does Autonomy Change the Nature of War, or Only Its Character?
posts.body:
Seminar 12,

This week's readings paired Clausewitz on friction, chance, and the culminating point with contemporary literature on autonomous systems, algorithmic decision support, and long-range precision fires.

Your issue for discussion:

A recurring claim in the current literature is that artificial intelligence and autonomous weapons are changing the nature of war rather than merely its character. Assess that claim.

Do not stop at asserting the distinction. If you argue the nature is immutable, tell the seminar what would falsify your position. State the observation that, if we made it, would force you to concede that the nature had changed. If you argue the nature is changing, identify which specific element of the nature is being displaced and by what mechanism.

Same standards. Initial post NLT Wednesday 2359. Two substantive peer responses NLT Sunday 2359. Q and A forum; post before you read.

A note on last week: the strongest exchanges in IFD 1 were the ones where somebody changed position under pressure. That is what this forum is for.

LtCol Halloran (Ret)

posts.author: Maj T. Okafor
posts.subject: Re: IFD 2: The nature is immutable, and here is what would falsify that
posts.body:
I argued the revisionist side last week and lost the argument fairly, so I want to be careful not to overcorrect. My position this week is that the nature is not changing, and I want to be precise about why.

Clausewitz's nature consists of violence, chance and friction, uncertainty, and subordination to political purpose. Autonomy attacks exactly one of these, and only partially. Machine speed compresses the observation and decision cycle and can reduce certain categories of friction, particularly those arising from human information processing limits. It does not remove friction; it relocates it. In my career field the friction moved into the model. Training data drift, adversarial spoofing, brittle performance outside the training distribution, and the integration seams between autonomous and human systems are all friction in Clausewitz's exact sense: the difference between war on paper and war in reality. An autonomous system that fails because it encountered a situation outside its distribution is a purer expression of friction than a supply column stuck in mud, because the failure is invisible until it matters.

What would falsify my position: a system that both selects and executes lethal action against a political adversary, at scale and over time, with no human political authority in the loop at any level, and which no human can halt. Not a delegated engagement authority within a human-set mission, which is what current systems represent. I mean violence that is genuinely not instrumental to any human political aim because no human is directing it toward one. That would sever the third leg from the human political community, and Clausewitz's definition of war as an instrument of policy would no longer describe the thing.

I do not think we are close to that. I do think the falsification condition is technically coherent, which is more than I could say for most claims in this debate.

Maj Okafor, USAF

posts.author: Maj D. Whitfield
posts.subject: Re: IFD 2: Immutable, but the interesting risk is on the political leg
posts.body:
The nature is not changing. But I think the seminar will spend its energy on the wrong leg, so let me put the risk where I think it actually is.

Most of the debate about AI and war focuses on violence and friction: will machines kill, will the fog lift. Those are character arguments. Precision munitions did not change the nature of war and neither will autonomy, for the same reason: they change how the violence is delivered, not that it is violence, uncertain, and political.

The leg worth watching is the political one, and the mechanism is cost. Clausewitz's system depends on war being expensive enough that the political authority must continuously judge whether the object is worth the effort. That judgment is the mechanism by which violence stays subordinate to policy. Now consider a sustained campaign conducted with attritable autonomous systems where the casualty cost to the initiating polity is near zero and the financial cost is a rounding error in a defense budget. The political authority is still in charge. But the feedback that disciplined its judgment has been substantially attenuated.

That is not a change in the nature of war. Political purpose is still present. It is a change in the reliability of the mechanism that keeps political purpose connected to reality, which may be the more dangerous thing precisely because it does not require any change in the nature to produce catastrophic outcomes.

My falsification condition is close to what I would expect from Maj Okafor: I would concede the nature had changed if the political object could be achieved by force without any human political community bearing risk, cost, or consequence, because at that point I am no longer sure the thing is a contest of wills at all.

Maj Whitfield, USMC

posts.author: LCDR P. Raghunathan
posts.subject: Re: IFD 2: The immutability claim is doing less work than we think
posts.body:
I want to make an argument that may be unpopular: the immutable nature position is true and also close to empty, and we should be honest about that.

Here is the problem. We have defined the nature of war at a level of abstraction so high that almost nothing could contradict it. War is violent, uncertain, and political. Any conflict that is not violent, uncertain, and political is by definition not war, so the claim is close to analytic. When we tell a wargaming audience that AI does not change the nature of war, we sound wise and we have said almost nothing operationally.

So let me try to make the claim earn its keep. The useful version is not that the nature is immutable but that the elements of the nature have characteristic quantities, and those can shift far enough to matter without crossing a categorical line. Friction has a magnitude. The decision cycle has a duration. The political authority's reaction time has a floor set by human cognition. If autonomy compresses engagement timelines below the interval required for a human political authority to deliberate, then policy has not been removed from war, but it has been structurally relegated to setting conditions in advance rather than judging in the moment.

Call that pre-commitment of policy. Policy is still present, so the nature is intact by the letter. But Clausewitz's whole account of the political leg is about continuous judgment, not a rule set loaded before the shooting starts. I think that is where the real argument is, and I think both the immutabilists and the revisionists talk past it.

What would falsify me: evidence that human political authority retains meaningful in-stride judgment at machine engagement speeds. I would genuinely like to be shown that.

LCDR Raghunathan, USN

posts.author: MAJ E. Vasquez-Ruiz
posts.subject: Re: IFD 2: Immutable, with a historical control
posts.body:
The nature is immutable, and I want to argue it by using history as a control rather than by asserting the distinction again.

Every technology we now regard as clearly a character change was described by its contemporaries as a change in the fundamental nature of war. The machine gun, the airplane, and the tank each produced serious literature claiming that war itself had become something categorically new. Douhet argued that airpower had rendered surface warfare and its logic obsolete. The atomic bomb produced the most credible version of this claim, and Brodie's argument that the military establishment's purpose had shifted from winning wars to averting them is the closest anyone has come to a genuine nature change.

And yet: Korea, Vietnam, the Falklands, the Gulf, Ukraine. Violence, friction, chance, and politics all present. The nuclear revolution changed the character so profoundly that it reorganized the international system, and the nature held. That is a strong prior. Autonomy is a smaller perturbation than nuclear weapons and the burden of proof on the revisionist side should be set accordingly.

My falsification condition is different from what I expect others will offer. I would concede if war ceased to be a contest between opposed wills, which is the element I take to be foundational and which none of the technology arguments touch. If autonomous systems fought each other with no human will engaged on either side, the activity would resemble war and would not be war. It would be an expensive industrial competition with kinetic effects. That is the line for me, and I note that it is a line about wills rather than about technology.

MAJ Vasquez-Ruiz, USA

posts.author: MAJ K. Nakamura
posts.subject: Re: IFD 2: What the PLA actually claims, and why it matters here
posts.body:
The claim in the Western literature that AI changes the nature of war is usually made loosely. The PLA version is more disciplined and I think it is worth putting in front of the seminar because it changes what we are arguing about.

Intelligentized warfare, as it appears in PLA writing, is generally not a claim that the nature of war has changed. It is a claim about which domain is decisive. The argument is that the contest has moved to the cognitive domain, and that the objective is to degrade the adversary's ability to decide before or instead of degrading his ability to fight. Some of the writing on cognitive domain operations goes further and describes victory achieved through the paralysis of the opponent's decision system rather than through the destruction of his forces.

If that is right, the interesting question is not whether the nature changed. It is whether their theory of victory and ours describe the same activity. A framework that targets will and decision directly is, ironically, closer to Clausewitz's contest of wills than our own attrition and precision-strike habits are.

My own position is that the nature is unchanged. What would falsify it for me is if the decisive contest could be resolved entirely without violence or the credible threat of it, at which point we would be discussing coercion and subversion rather than war. Capt Boone's cartel bribery problem from last week turns out to be the same question in a different suit, which I did not expect.

MAJ Nakamura, USA

posts.author: Capt S. Lindquist
posts.subject: Re: IFD 2: Unchanged nature, and an attempt to do better than last week
posts.body:
MAJ Nakamura and Capt Pierce both pushed me last week on leaning too hard on doctrine to settle a question doctrine was not written to settle. The criticism was fair, so I am going to try to argue from evidence instead.

My position is that the nature is unchanged. My evidence is the intelligence problem specifically. If AI were lifting the fog of war, we would expect uncertainty about adversary intent to decrease as sensing and processing improve. My experience does not support that. Collection volume has grown enormously and the analytical bottleneck has not moved, because the hard problem was never collection. It was intent, and intent lives in an adversary's head and is deliberately concealed. More data has produced more competing hypotheses, not fewer. Uncertainty is being generated at least as fast as it is being resolved.

MCDP 1 is still where I would go for the framing of uncertainty as an enduring attribute, but I am citing it as a description that matches what I have observed rather than as the reason the answer is correct. That is the distinction I missed last week.

Falsification: I would concede the nature had changed if an adversary's future intent became reliably predictable rather than merely estimable, because uncertainty is the element of the nature I would expect automation to attack first. I do not expect that to happen, but it is testable and it is the thing I watch for.

Capt Lindquist, USMC

posts.author: Capt M. Boone
posts.subject: Re: IFD 2: Unchanged, and last week changed how I got here
posts.body:
Unchanged nature. But I want to answer the falsification question honestly rather than pick the easy version.

The test I would apply is the one thing I actually know from experience: friction always reappears somewhere downstream of wherever you removed it. We got better ISR and the friction moved to processing. We got better comms and the friction moved to bandwidth and to the fact that everyone above me could now watch and interject. Every capability that removed friction at one point in the system created it at another. So my falsification condition is a war in which friction is removed at one point and does not reappear anywhere else. If someone can show me a system where the total friction actually went down rather than moved, I will reconsider.

I also want to flag something about my own reasoning. Last week I said the trinity was a strategic tool with no company-level application, and LCDR Raghunathan pointed out that I had used it operationally in the same post without noticing. I think I do that a lot: use the theory and then claim it is not useful. What I am taking from this course so far is less that I am learning new frameworks and more that I am learning to notice the ones I was already using badly.

Capt Boone, USMC

posts.author: Capt A. Pierce
posts.subject: Re: IFD 2: Initial post
posts.body:
My position is that AI is changing the character of war and not its nature.

Capt Lindquist challenged me last week to take a position on a specific step instead of just stating the conclusion, so I will try. The step here is whether autonomy removes uncertainty. I do not think it does, because uncertainty in war comes from the enemy actively hiding things and not just from us lacking sensors. A better sensor does not fix a deliberate deception. So the uncertainty element of the nature stays even if the technology improves.

What would falsify my position is if we ever got to a point where the enemy could not surprise us at all.

Capt Pierce, USMC

posts.author: Capt R. Deleon
posts.subject: Re: IFD 2: Initial post
posts.body:
Nature does not change, character does. In aviation we have gotten better sensors and better weapons every decade and the fight still comes down to a person deciding whether to pull the trigger with incomplete information. Autonomy will not change that, it will just move the incomplete information somewhere else. Falsification would be if the machines started deciding what the war was about.

Capt Deleon, USMC

posts.author: MAJ E. Vasquez-Ruiz
posts.subject: Re: IFD 2: On pre-commitment of policy
posts.body:
LCDR Raghunathan, pre-commitment of policy is the most useful thing anyone has put on the table in two weeks and I want to test it rather than praise it.

Here is my worry. Pre-commitment is not new. Mobilization timetables in 1914 were pre-commitment of policy: once the schedules started, the political authority's in-stride judgment was structurally subordinated to a rule set loaded in advance, and Europe went to war partly because nobody could stop the trains. Nuclear launch-on-warning is a purer case. If pre-commitment already produced the effect you describe, twice, at civilizational scale, before any autonomy existed, then it is not a consequence of machine speed. It is a recurring feature of what happens when the tempo of military systems outruns the tempo of political deliberation.

That actually helps your argument in one way and hurts it in another. It helps because it shows the mechanism is real and has historical evidence behind it. It hurts because it means autonomy is not doing anything categorically new; it is doing the 1914 thing faster and at lower thresholds.

So I would reframe: not pre-commitment as a novel phenomenon, but the threshold at which pre-commitment becomes necessary dropping from general war to routine engagement. That is a change in frequency and level, which is character. But I concede it is character in a way that could produce a strategic outcome indistinguishable from a nature change, which is a distinction I am not entirely comfortable with.

posts.author: LCDR P. Raghunathan
posts.subject: Re: IFD 2: On pre-commitment of policy
posts.body:
MAJ Vasquez-Ruiz, the 1914 parallel is exactly right and I should have found it myself.

I accept the reframe with one amendment. In 1914 the pre-commitment was legible: the timetables were written down, human beings had authored them, and the political authority could in principle read them and understand what it was authorizing. Bethmann-Hollweg's failure was a failure of will and comprehension, not of access. The amendment I want is that pre-commitment through a learned model is not legible in the same way. The rule set is not authored, it is trained, and its behavior at the edges of its distribution is not fully known to anyone including its builders. So the political authority is pre-committing to a decision rule it cannot fully inspect.

Is that a nature change? No. Political purpose is still present and still human. But it means the political leg is now connected to the violence through a mechanism whose behavior is opaque to the authority using it, and I do not think Clausewitz's account has a place for that. He assumes the instrument is comprehensible to the hand holding it.

That is my actual position now and it is the third one I have held this week, which I think is the correct number.

posts.author: Maj T. Okafor
posts.subject: Re: IFD 2: On the cost attenuation argument
posts.body:
Maj Whitfield, I want to push on the cost argument because I think you have the mechanism slightly wrong and the correction makes your case stronger.

You frame it as the initiating polity bearing near-zero cost. But cheap attritable systems are cheap for both sides, and the historical record on cheap force is not that it lowers the cost of war. It is that it lowers the threshold of entry, which raises the frequency of conflict and eventually the aggregate cost. Ukraine is the live case: a several-hundred-dollar FPV drone servicing a multi-million dollar vehicle did not make that war cheap. It made it more attritional and it drove both sides into an industrial production competition.

So the political authority may not experience attenuated cost at all. It may experience cost arriving in an unfamiliar currency, industrial capacity and component supply rather than casualties, on a timeline its budget process is not built to read.

That is worse for your peace of mind and better for your argument, because it means the feedback disciplining the political judgment is not weakened so much as mistranslated. And a signal the political authority misreads is more dangerous than one it does not receive at all, because it produces confident wrong decisions rather than cautious ones.

posts.author: Maj D. Whitfield
posts.subject: Re: IFD 2: On the cost attenuation argument
posts.body:
Maj Okafor, I am taking the correction. Mistranslated rather than attenuated is more accurate and it fits the Ukraine evidence better than my framing did.

As a logistician I should have gotten there first, and I think I missed it because I was reasoning about the political leg in isolation instead of asking what actually reaches the political authority and in what form. The signal that disciplines policy is not cost as such, it is cost the authority can perceive, attribute, and act on within its decision cycle. Casualties are perceptible, attributable, and politically legible. Depletion of a magazine of loitering munitions against a production base that cannot replace them for eighteen months is none of those things until the moment it is decisive.

Which means the culminating point becomes much harder to see from the political level, and Clausewitz is quite clear about what happens to a belligerent who does not recognize his culminating point. That is a character change with strategic consequences, not a nature change, but it is the specific mechanism I would brief if anyone asked me why this matters.

posts.author: Capt S. Lindquist
posts.subject: Re: IFD 2: On cognitive domain operations
posts.body:
MAJ Nakamura, your point that a theory targeting decision directly is closer to Clausewitz's contest of wills than our own habits are is uncomfortable and I think it is correct.

From the intelligence side I would add a caution about how we translate their writing. Doctrinal literature is aspirational and institutional. What appears in PLA journals about cognitive domain operations reflects what a faction wants funded as much as what the force can do, and we have a long history of reading adversary doctrine as capability. That does not make your point wrong. It means the claim that they have moved the decisive contest to the cognitive domain is a claim about their theory, not evidence about their practice, and I would want to see those separated before anyone builds a program around it.

Where I fully agree is that if their theory of victory targets our decision system, then uncertainty and friction are not obstacles they are working around. They are the weapons. That reframes friction from a condition we endure into a thing an adversary manufactures deliberately, and I do not think our planning treats it that way.

posts.author: Capt A. Mills
posts.subject: Re: IFD 2: Late initial post
posts.body:
Late again, apologies. Field exercise support.

I think AI changes the character of war but not the nature. War will still be violent, uncertain, and political no matter what technology is used. The falsification would be if war stopped being political.

Capt Mills, USMC

posts.author: MAJ K. Nakamura
posts.subject: Re: IFD 2: Friction relocates rather than disappears
posts.body:
Capt Boone, your falsification test is the most practical one in the thread and I want to name why.

Everyone else, including me, offered a falsification condition that is a thought experiment: no human will engaged, no political aim, perfect prediction. Those are unobservable in any realistic timeframe, which makes them safe. Yours is measurable. Total friction in a system before and after a capability is introduced is at least in principle something you could assess, and it could come out against you.

On your second paragraph, about noticing frameworks you were already using badly: that is the more valuable observation and I would not let it sit at the bottom of the post. The gap between the theory an officer can recite and the theory an officer actually reasons with is where most of our professional failures live. You have caught yourself twice in two weeks. That is the point of the seminar.

posts.author: Capt M. Boone
posts.subject: Re: IFD 2: Friction moved into the model
posts.body:
Maj Okafor, the line about friction moving into the model is the clearest thing I have read in this course and it matches something I saw without having language for it.

We had a targeting support tool that worked well in the environment it was built for and got quietly unreliable when the pattern of life changed. Nobody could tell you when it stopped being trustworthy. It just gradually was not, and the people relying on it did not know because the outputs looked exactly the same. That is worse than a truck in the mud, because the truck tells you it is stuck.

So your point that the failure is invisible until it matters is not a technical footnote. It is the operational problem. Friction you can see, you can plan around. Friction that presents as confidence is a different category of thing and I do not think our staff processes have a way to account for it.

posts.author: Maj D. Whitfield
posts.subject: Re: IFD 2: On intelligentized warfare
posts.body:
MAJ Nakamura, I want to connect your post to the logistics problem because I think the cognitive domain framing has a materiel consequence nobody has raised.

If an adversary's theory of victory is to paralyze our decision system rather than destroy our forces, then the highest-value target set is not the force. It is the mechanism that tells the force what is true: the common operating picture, the sustainment visibility systems, the readiness reporting that a commander uses to know what he actually has. In my world, corrupted or delayed logistics data does not look like an attack. It looks like a bad week. A commander who believes he has thirty days of a critical class of supply and has nine will culminate without ever recognizing that he was attacked.

That is the same structure Capt Boone described in the targeting tool and the same structure Maj Okafor described as friction inside the model. Three of us have now independently arrived at deception of our own confidence as the mechanism that matters, from three different career fields. Either that is convergent evidence or it is a shared blind spot in how our generation was trained, and I cannot tell which from inside it.

posts.author: Capt A. Pierce
posts.subject: Re: IFD 2: Immutable, with a historical control
posts.body:
MAJ Vasquez-Ruiz, the point about every technology being described as a nature change by its contemporaries is useful and I had not thought about it as a pattern before. The Douhet example makes it concrete.

One question. If people have been wrong about this every time, is there a risk we assume they are wrong this time as well and miss it when it is actually happening? Your nuclear example seems like the closest anyone came to being right.

posts.author: Maj T. Okafor
posts.subject: Re: IFD 2: On the intelligence bottleneck
posts.body:
Capt Lindquist, your falsification condition is better constructed than mine and I want to name why, because it is a distinction I use constantly at work and did not apply to my own post.

You set the line at intent becoming reliably predictable rather than merely estimable. That is the correct line, because it separates the two things automation actually does. Machine learning is very good at extrapolating patterns from observed behavior and structurally incapable of accessing a decision that has not been made yet. An adversary who has not decided has no signal to detect, and no amount of collection fixes that, because the thing does not exist.

The risk in my field is the opposite of the one you flag. Not that we fail to predict, but that we produce a confident probability against an unformed decision and the consumer reads the confidence rather than the estimate. That is your uncertainty problem arriving disguised as its own solution.

posts.author: MAJ E. Vasquez-Ruiz
posts.subject: Re: IFD 2: Immutable, with a historical control
posts.body:
Capt Pierce, that is a real objection to my own argument and it deserves a direct answer.

Yes, there is that risk, and it has a name: the historical prior can become an excuse for not looking. My defense is that the prior is not doing all the work. I also offered a falsification condition, the contest of wills, that is independent of the historical pattern. If the prior were my only argument, your objection would be fatal, because past false alarms genuinely are weak evidence about the current case.

The honest version of my position is that the base rate justifies a demanding burden of proof, not a dismissal. What would worry me is if I found myself rejecting a specific piece of evidence by pointing at the pattern rather than by engaging the evidence. That is the failure mode you have identified and I will watch for it.

Good question. That is the kind of push I was hoping for on that post.

posts.author: Capt R. Deleon
posts.subject: Re: IFD 2: Unchanged nature
posts.body: Capt Lindquist, concur. The point that more collection has produced more competing hypotheses rather than fewer matches what I have seen from the aviation side. Good post.

posts.author: Capt R. Deleon
posts.subject: Re: IFD 2: Immutable, but the interesting risk is on the political leg
posts.body: Maj Whitfield, good post. The cost point makes sense to me.

posts.author: LtCol (Ret) J. Halloran
posts.subject: Faculty comment: Three threads worth pulling
posts.body:
Seminar 12, this was a stronger week than last and the reason is specific: several of you argued against your own posts. LCDR Raghunathan held three positions in five days and each was better than the one before it. Maj Whitfield took a correction from Maj Okafor and rebuilt his mechanism around it. MAJ Vasquez-Ruiz answered a challenge to her own historical prior by conceding the weakness rather than defending the post. That is what intellectual honesty looks like in writing and it is harder than being right the first time.

Again, I am not adjudicating. Three things to pull on.

First. Almost every one of you converged on the same structure: the nature is intact by the letter, and something important is happening to the mechanism connecting the political leg to the violence. Pre-commitment, mistranslated cost, opaque decision rules, friction that presents as confidence. You reached that from four different directions without coordinating, which should make you suspicious in a productive way. Either you have collectively found something, or the seminar shares an assumption none of you has stated. Which is it? I want somebody to try to falsify the consensus rather than add to it.

Second, to MAJ Vasquez-Ruiz and MAJ Nakamura. Both of you set your falsification condition at the contest of wills. Consider a war in which one side's will is genuine and the other side's political community is disengaged, casualty-insulated, and effectively unaware the war is being fought. Is that still a contest of wills, and if it is only one-sided, what does your condition actually rule out? I am not sure your line is where you think it is.

Third, to Capt Deleon and Capt Mills. Both of you have now stated the correct distinction twice and stopped there. Capt Deleon, your aviation observation about the trigger decision with incomplete information is the beginning of a real argument and you abandoned it in the same sentence you made it. Capt Mills, your posts have arrived after the discussion has largely concluded, which means the seminar has not had the benefit of your thinking and you have not had the benefit of the exchange. Both of you: pick one classmate's post you disagree with, even slightly, and tell them why. Not agreement. Disagreement, in writing, with a reason. That is the assignment for the extension.

Forum remains open through Wednesday.

LtCol Halloran (Ret)

posts.author: Capt S. Lindquist
posts.subject: Re: IFD 2: On the falsification condition
posts.body:
Maj Okafor, I think your falsification condition is the most rigorous one offered and I also think it is unreachable in a way that should worry you.

You require a system that selects and executes lethal action with no human political authority in the loop at any level, and which no human can halt. Any real system will have a human somewhere in its history: it was procured, fielded, and released by someone. So the condition can never be met, which means it cannot do the falsifying work you want it to do. It is the same problem LCDR Raghunathan identified in the general immutability claim, and I do not think your version escapes it.

The usable version might be a threshold rather than an absolute. Not no human authority anywhere, but no human authority capable of intervening within the interval in which the decisive effects occur. That is observable and it could come out against you, which is what a falsification condition is supposed to do.

posts.author: LCDR P. Raghunathan
posts.subject: Re: Faculty comment: attempting to falsify our own consensus
posts.body:
Sir, taking the first question, and I think the shared unstated assumption is this: we have all assumed that continuous political judgment during a war is normal and that its erosion is a departure.

I am not sure that is historically true. How much in-stride political judgment was actually exercised at Verdun, or in the strategic bombing campaign after the target lists were set, or during the six weeks after the Schlieffen deployment began? The pattern may be that political authority sets conditions, releases the instrument, and reasserts control at decision points that are rare rather than continuous. If so, the mechanism we are all worried about breaking has been intermittent the entire time, and what autonomy changes is the length of the interval, not the existence of the gap.

That falsifies our consensus in the form we stated it. What survives is narrower and I think more defensible: the interval between meaningful political judgments is shortening relative to the pace at which irreversible effects accumulate. That is a claim about ratios rather than about the presence or absence of political control, and it is the version I would be willing to defend.

LCDR Raghunathan, USN

posts.author: MAJ K. Nakamura
posts.subject: Re: Faculty comment: on the one-sided contest of wills
posts.body:
Sir, your second question does damage to my falsification condition and I do not think I can save it in its current form.

You have described a real category, not a hypothetical one. A great power conducting sustained strikes against a distant adversary, with a domestic population that is disengaged and unaffected, is close to what several of our own campaigns looked like from the other side. If I hold that a genuine contest of wills is required for the activity to be war, I am committed to saying those were not wars. I am not willing to say that.

So the condition has to be reformulated. The candidate I would offer is that war requires a contest of wills between the belligerent political authorities, not between their populations. The disengaged population is a fact about how the polity organizes consent, not about whether a will is engaged. That preserves the category and it survives your case.

But it costs me something, and I want to name the cost rather than hide it. It concedes that a polity can conduct war with its political will engaged and its people disengaged, which is precisely the condition Maj Whitfield warned about on the cost side. My reformulation rules his danger case in as war rather than ruling it out. That may be the correct answer and it is not a comfortable one.

MAJ Nakamura, USA

posts.author: Capt R. Deleon
posts.subject: Re: Faculty comment: taking the disagreement assignment
posts.body:
Sir, taking the assignment. My disagreement is with LCDR Raghunathan.

The argument that human political authority cannot exercise judgment at machine speed treats the engagement timeline as the timeline that matters. In aviation, the fast part was always faster than any deliberation could keep up with. Nobody calls the White House during a merge. What made those engagements political was the ROE, the target list, and the commander's intent set before I ever launched, and I want to argue that this was never a degraded form of political control. It was the normal form. The political judgment happened at the pace political judgment happens, and the execution happened at the pace execution happens, and they were connected by rules and by trust in the person executing.

Where I will concede ground is that the person executing was accountable and could be asked afterward why he did what he did. A model cannot be asked. So my disagreement is narrower than I thought when I started typing it: the speed is not the new thing, the accountability gap is. Which I think is close to where LCDR Raghunathan ended up anyway, so maybe this is agreement arriving by a different road.

This took me longer than my original post did, which is probably the point.

Capt Deleon, USMC

posts.author: Capt A. Mills
posts.subject: Re: Faculty comment
posts.body:
Sir, understood on the timing, I will get ahead of it next week.

I disagree with Capt Boone that friction always reappears somewhere else. In engineering we have removed friction from things permanently, for example a bridge that used to take a day to emplace and now takes hours. That friction did not move anywhere, it is just gone. So I think some friction can actually be removed.

Capt Mills, USMC

posts.author: Capt M. Boone
posts.subject: Re: Faculty comment
posts.body:
Capt Mills, that is a fair challenge and I want to answer it seriously because I think it is closer than you might expect.

The bridge goes in faster. Agreed. But the friction I am talking about is the whole system's, not the task's. Faster gap crossing means the scheme of maneuver now assumes the crossing happens on time, which means the plan has less slack, which means the consequences of the crossing being contested are larger than they used to be. The engineer's friction went down and the operation's tolerance for anything going wrong went down with it. Whether that is net removal or relocation is a real question and I do not think my claim is proven.

Good push. First one you have made and it landed on the weakest part of my argument.
